patterns.structural_signature: The executing process exposes a control channel that remains live while it runs; commands on that channel (pause, substitute a parameter, resume, abort) take effect on the in-flight run rather than queueing for the next one. The system therefore holds partial state that is valid to inspect and to modify mid-execution.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the run can be suspended, redirected or exited mid-flight
patterns.description: the run can be suspended, redirected or exited mid-flight

patterns.short_summary: The system opens with a concrete proposal rather than an empty field; the user reacts to it; the reaction becomes an input that yields a revised version of the same artifact.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Defines repeated co-creation around one persistent artifact.
patterns.definition: The system opens with a concrete proposal rather than an empty field; the user reacts to it; the reaction becomes an input that yields a revised version of the same artifact. The cycle repeats without returning to a blank specification.
patterns.structural_signature: A cycle in the control graph in which the previous output is carried into the next call together with the user's critique. Artifact identity persists across iterations — the next state is an edit of the current one, not an independent draw — so the state at round n depends on rounds 1 through n-1.
patterns.source_pattern_name: propose-critique-revise iteration loop over the same artifact
patterns.description: propose-critique-revise iteration loop over the same artifact

patterns.short_summary: Alongside the generative route, the interface keeps a route by which the user authors the same material directly: a free-text field, editable nodes, a custom operation, a user-added prompt.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Preserves choice between direct creation and AI assistance throughout the task.
patterns.definition: Alongside the generative route, the interface keeps a route by which the user authors the same material directly: a free-text field, editable nodes, a custom operation, a user-added prompt. Neither route is a fallback mode; both are available at the same time.
patterns.structural_signature: Two input routes converge on the same artifact slot — one generated, one hand-authored — with no mode switch between them, and the artifact can record contributions from both. Removing the generator leaves the interface still operable for that slot; the slot's schema is identical whichever route filled it.
patterns.source_pattern_name: manual authoring path retained beside the generated one
patterns.description: manual authoring path retained beside the generated one

patterns.short_summary: Every system-produced item arrives with the same small, closed set of actions attached to it, so the user's response to any suggestion is drawn from a uniform vocabulary.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Attaches consistent controls such as accept, edit, regenerate, insert, or ignore to each item.
patterns.definition: Every system-produced item arrives with the same small, closed set of actions attached to it, so the user's response to any suggestion is drawn from a uniform vocabulary. The unit of disposition is the individual item, not the batch. The specific set varies by system — accept/regenerate/edit, replace/abstract, insert/ignore — but its fixity and its per-item attachment are what the pattern names.
patterns.structural_signature: Each generated item is rendered with a co-located control group whose members are identical across items and constant across the session; activating a member commits a disposition for that item alone and leaves other items untouched. The set is enumerable and closed, and there is no path for disposing of items that is not in the set.
patterns.source_pattern_name: fixed disposition set offered on every suggestion
patterns.description: fixed disposition set offered on every suggestion

patterns.short_summary: A continuous artifact is partitioned into named units, and each unit becomes an independently addressable object.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Gives artifact parts persistent identities and per-unit controls.
patterns.definition: A continuous artifact is partitioned into named units, and each unit becomes an independently addressable object. Operations that would otherwise apply to the whole — editing, regenerating, tagging, attributing — apply per unit. The partition is materialized on screen, and its boundaries may themselves be adjustable.
patterns.structural_signature: A single artifact is divided into a set of non-overlapping parts, each given an identity (a name, a type label, a card, a row). Each part carries its own handles, so the artifact has as many operation targets as it has parts, all simultaneously present. Segmentation may be automatic or user-adjusted, but the resulting units persist as the unit of interaction rather than dissolving back into the whole.
patterns.source_pattern_name: segmented into discrete units, each individually addressable
patterns.description: segmented into discrete units, each individually addressable

patterns.short_summary: The model's output is not the artifact the user wanted but a generator of it: code, a hierarchical program, or a parameterized template that must be executed or instantiated to yield the artifact.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Makes an editable generator or template the control surface for downstream artifacts.
patterns.definition: The model's output is not the artifact the user wanted but a generator of it: code, a hierarchical program, or a parameterized template that must be executed or instantiated to yield the artifact. The user's subsequent edits act on that intermediate producer, and re-running it with different arguments yields a family of artifacts. The finished object is downstream of the model's output, not identical to it.
patterns.structural_signature: Pipeline: prompt → program/template → execution → artifact. The program is a first-class, addressable object with named parts (functions, operators, parameters) and it persists after the artifact is rendered, so re-execution under different bindings is available without re-invoking the model. Diagnostic: changing an argument changes the artifact with no new generation call. Transplants to any output medium with an executable description language — layout, geometry, music, documents.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the model emits a program or parameterized template rather than the finished artifact
patterns.description: the model emits a program or parameterized template rather than the finished artifact The output is a generator of the artifact - code or a parameterised template - not the artifact itself.

patterns.short_summary: The system pre-populates the working artifact with generated content that occupies its final position, and the user's task begins from that filled state.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Places generated material directly in its final editable surface.
patterns.definition: The system pre-populates the working artifact with generated content that occupies its final position, and the user's task begins from that filled state. The content is directly editable where it sits rather than being accepted or rejected as a block. The starting point is a draft, not a blank.
patterns.structural_signature: Generated material is written into the artifact's own slots before the user acts, so the artifact is non-empty at first contact. Edit affordances operate on the material in place — the same handles the user would have for their own content — and there is no separate accept step gating it into the artifact. The generated portion may be marked (highlighted as adaptable, listed as alternatives) but it is already committed.
patterns.source_pattern_name: system-filled content left editable in place
patterns.description: system-filled content left editable in place

patterns.short_summary: Two or more views of the same underlying object are shown at once, each of them editable, and an edit in any one propagates to the others.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Provides bidirectional editing across multiple views of the same object.
patterns.definition: Two or more views of the same underlying object are shown at once, each of them editable, and an edit in any one propagates to the others. Neither view is subordinate: the user may work in whichever is convenient and the system reconciles them. The conversion runs in both directions rather than compiling one representation into the other.
patterns.structural_signature: A shared model backs multiple concurrently displayed representations; each representation has write access to the model; a propagation step updates the sibling representations after any write. The loop is closed — starting in representation A, converting to B, and editing B returns a valid state in A.
patterns.source_pattern_name: two representations kept synchronized and editable from either side
patterns.description: two representations kept synchronized and editable from either side

patterns.short_summary: The user designates a sub-extent of the artifact and the generative operation applies to exactly that extent.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Uses selections, masks, or spatial marks to delimit generation.
patterns.definition: The user designates a sub-extent of the artifact and the generative operation applies to exactly that extent. What lies outside the designation is not rewritten. The mark carries no content of its own: it says where, not what.
patterns.structural_signature: The artifact admits addressing of proper sub-extents (a text selection, a painted mask, a stroke set, a pane, a spatial region). A designation act records one such extent as the current scope; the operation's write set is bounded by it and the complement is held fixed; the result is composited back into the original at the marked position. The scope is re-designatable and the operation is otherwise the same regardless of which extent is chosen.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the operation scoped to the region or location the user marks
patterns.description: the operation scoped to the region or location the user marks

patterns.short_summary: A finished artifact that the system did not produce is decomposed back into an underlying structure — data table, encoding spec, component graph, layered representation — and that recovered structure becomes the object the user manipulates.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Exposes recovered structure such as components, layers, data, or encoding specifications.
patterns.definition: A finished artifact that the system did not produce is decomposed back into an underlying structure — data table, encoding spec, component graph, layered representation — and that recovered structure becomes the object the user manipulates. The original rendered form is treated as output whose source has been lost and must be reconstructed. Editing happens on the recovered structure, not on the surface.
patterns.structural_signature: An ingestion step takes a rendered or compiled artifact and emits a structured representation of it (typed nodes, fields, layers, specs); that representation is bound to the editing surface, and changes to it re-render the artifact. The recovery is inverse to the artifact's own production pipeline, and the representation is richer than the surface it was derived from.
patterns.source_pattern_name: an existing artifact reverse-engineered into an editable representation
patterns.description: an existing artifact reverse-engineered into an editable representation

patterns.short_summary: The sequence of conversational turns is governed by an authored control structure — a finite state machine, a protocol tree, a fixed phase sequence, a structured prompting scheme — rather than by the model's turn-by-turn discretion.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Defines allowable conversational states and transitions.
patterns.definition: The sequence of conversational turns is governed by an authored control structure — a finite state machine, a protocol tree, a fixed phase sequence, a structured prompting scheme — rather than by the model's turn-by-turn discretion. The structure is a designed object, sometimes authorable by non-programmers.
patterns.structural_signature: A graph or ordered stage list exists as an inspectable (often editable) object: nodes carry what the agent says or does, edges carry conditions evaluated on the interlocutor's response. The current node is persistent state, and a transition is computed at every turn, so the reachable next turns are a function of position in the structure.
patterns.source_pattern_name: explicit control structure over dialogue turns
patterns.description: explicit control structure over dialogue turns

patterns.short_summary: Work advances through an ordered series of stages that is fixed by the designer before the user arrives.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Organizes work as a stable designer-authored sequence.
patterns.definition: Work advances through an ordered series of stages that is fixed by the designer before the user arrives. The interface makes the ordering visible and moves the user along it, one stage at a time. Iteration within a stage or between neighbouring stages may be permitted, but the sequence itself is not authored by the user.
patterns.structural_signature: A stage list S1…Sn exists in the system independent of any particular input, and each stage has its own module, section, or screen. The surface encodes the order (sections laid out in workflow order, a guided sequence of overlays, a chain of modules each consuming the previous one's output), and advancement is by completing or passing a stage rather than by free navigation. The number and identity of stages are constant across runs.
patterns.source_pattern_name: fixed staged pipeline the user is walked through
patterns.description: fixed staged pipeline the user is walked through

patterns.short_summary: Prior states and actions are retained as first-class records rather than discarded when superseded.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Makes prior states available for restoration, continuation, branching, or playback.
patterns.definition: Prior states and actions are retained as first-class records rather than discarded when superseded. The interface exposes them as a navigable set the user can return to, resume from, or play back in time order. History is an object in the system, not just a side effect of use.
patterns.structural_signature: Every state change appends an addressable record (a version, a modification entry, an accept/reject/edit event, a timestamped frame). The interface renders the record set as a navigable structure — a list, a stream, a timeline — and supports two operations over it: returning to a past state and continuing from there, and traversing the sequence in temporal order. Records survive the session and the same view may serve live and retrospective inspection.
patterns.source_pattern_name: revisitable history, versioning and replay
patterns.description: revisitable history, versioning and replay

patterns.short_summary: A goal supplied at runtime is broken into smaller sub-parts, and the parts are produced or handled serially rather than in one shot.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Turns a runtime goal into inspectable, sequential sub-tasks.
patterns.definition: A goal supplied at runtime is broken into smaller sub-parts, and the parts are produced or handled serially rather than in one shot. The decomposition is derived from the particular goal, so its shape varies with the input. Each part surfaces as its own step that can be inspected or edited before the next is taken.
patterns.structural_signature: An input goal is transformed into an ordered list of sub-parts whose length and identity are computed per input (by the system, the user, or both). Each sub-part is executed or generated separately, in sequence, and appears as a discrete step in the interface; the final artifact is assembled from the parts. The sequence exists only for this goal — a different goal yields a different sequence.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the task decomposed into parts handled one at a time
patterns.description: the task decomposed into parts handled one at a time

patterns.short_summary: The interaction surface is a vertically scrolling transcript of alternating turns with a persistent composition area anchored below it.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Uses an append-only transcript above a persistent composition region.
patterns.definition: The interaction surface is a vertically scrolling transcript of alternating turns with a persistent composition area anchored below it. The transcript is the record and the display at once: earlier turns remain addressable by scrolling, and new turns append to the end. Nothing about the layout is specialized to the task; the same surface would serve any turn-taking exchange.
patterns.structural_signature: Two regions: an append-only scrollable list of turn elements attributed to a speaker, and a fixed input region containing a text field plus a send affordance. New content enters at one end; the viewport auto-follows or can be scrolled back; history persists in the same region it was produced in. This is fully statable without reference to what the turns are about, which is precisely why it recurs across unrelated domains.
patterns.source_pattern_name: scrollable chat-log surface with a text-entry area
patterns.description: scrollable chat-log surface with a text-entry area

patterns.short_summary: The system's activity is rendered within the work surface itself — as cursors, marks, live strokes, or attached companions — instead of being confined to a separate conversation panel.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Renders agent cursors, marks, strokes, or companions in the artifact's coordinate space.
patterns.definition: The system's activity is rendered within the work surface itself — as cursors, marks, live strokes, or attached companions — instead of being confined to a separate conversation panel. The user sees where the agent is and what it is touching while they continue to work in the same space. Presence cues are persistent and positioned relative to the artifact's content.
patterns.structural_signature: Agent state is drawn in the same coordinate space as the user's content, anchored to specific locations or to the pointer, and updates while the user is acting rather than only between turns. There is no separate container that owns the agent; removing the artifact view would remove the agent's visible form.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the agent's presence and actions shown inside the shared artifact
patterns.description: the agent's presence and actions shown inside the shared artifact

patterns.short_summary: A free-form conversational channel is live at the same time as a non-conversational artifact the user is attending to, and the turns are about that artifact.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Keeps an artifact and a conversation about it simultaneously available.
patterns.definition: A free-form conversational channel is live at the same time as a non-conversational artifact the user is attending to, and the turns are about that artifact. The artifact persists on display; the dialogue neither replaces it nor is required to advance it.
patterns.structural_signature: Two concurrently live regions (possibly on two devices): one holds a persistent artifact that is not consumed by the exchange, the other accepts an unbounded number of user-authored natural-language turns scoped to that artifact. Removing the dialogue channel leaves the artifact usable; removing the artifact leaves the dialogue without a referent.
patterns.source_pattern_name: open dialogue running alongside the artifact being viewed
patterns.description: open dialogue running alongside the artifact being viewed

patterns.short_summary: The same content is made available under two different presentation or interaction disciplines, and a selection determines which is in force.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Provides switchable interaction disciplines over one content payload.
patterns.definition: The same content is made available under two different presentation or interaction disciplines, and a selection determines which is in force. The modes differ in how the content is reached and acted on, not in what the content is. Only one mode operates at a time.
patterns.structural_signature: One content payload, two renderings with distinct interaction rules (push stream vs. pull query; predetermined navigation vs. free-form questioning; freeform text vs. structured fields; whole-document vs. extracted-terms conditioning), and a mode selector that makes one active. The modes are alternatives at the same point in the flow — either can serve the same user need — and switching between them does not change the underlying content. In several members the two modes are never both available to the same user; there the selector is the experimenter's assignment rather than a control (see the review flag).
patterns.source_pattern_name: two alternative presentation modes for the same content
patterns.description: two alternative presentation modes for the same content

patterns.short_summary: Task stages that were previously carried out in distinct tools, windows, or databases are placed inside one environment where they share state.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Consolidates previously separate tools or windows into one state-sharing workspace.
patterns.definition: Task stages that were previously carried out in distinct tools, windows, or databases are placed inside one environment where they share state. The consolidation itself, rather than any individual stage, is what the design claims.
patterns.structural_signature: One application shell containing two or more stages of a workflow whose state is shared, such that the output of one stage is directly addressable in another with no export/import step. Only half of this is observable in the artifact — several stage regions plus shared state; the "previously separate" half is a claim about prior tooling, and cannot be read off the interface.
patterns.source_pattern_name: successive workflow stages sharing state in a single environment
patterns.description: successive workflow stages sharing state in a single environment

patterns.short_summary: The generative capability is attached to a host artifact that the system did not author — a third-party application, a web page, a chat client, an established workflow.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Anchors AI functions to identifiable locations in a host surface.
patterns.definition: The generative capability is attached to a host artifact that the system did not author — a third-party application, a web page, a chat client, an established workflow. The host keeps its own structure and remains usable without the addition. The design move is the attachment point: where in the host the capability is inserted.
patterns.structural_signature: Two separable layers exist: a pre-existing host surface with its own controls and content, and an added layer (plugin, browser extension overlay, injected step, docked component) that renders generated content into or beside the host. The added layer is anchored to identifiable host locations — particular spans of host content, particular stages of the host's flow, particular composition steps — and the anchoring, not the generation, is what the paper specifies. Detaching the layer leaves the host intact.
patterns.source_pattern_name: assistance grafted into an existing tool, page or workflow
patterns.description: assistance grafted into an existing tool, page or workflow

patterns.short_summary: The screen is divided into a fixed number of persistent regions, each with an assigned function that does not change during use.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Assigns stable roles to persistent workspace regions.
patterns.definition: The screen is divided into a fixed number of persistent regions, each with an assigned function that does not change during use. The partition is stated as a design decision: which functions get their own region, and where each sits. Regions may differ in what they permit, for instance which of them accepts typing.
patterns.structural_signature: A stable spatial decomposition of one workspace into n named regions, each bound to a function (input, corpus, codebook, canvas, generated output, controls). Region identity and position persist across the session; content changes inside a region but its role does not. Spatial arrangement may encode something further — process order, or an editability asymmetry between regions.
patterns.source_pattern_name: workspace partitioned into fixed functional panels
patterns.description: workspace partitioned into fixed functional panels

patterns.short_summary: A character specification — a name, personality, social role, or narrative voice — is attached to the generative agent and held constant across its turns.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Establishes a persistent social role, voice, or perspective for the AI.
patterns.definition: A character specification — a name, personality, social role, or narrative voice — is attached to the generative agent and held constant across its turns. It is treated as a design element that can be set, swapped, or compared, independent of the task the agent performs.
patterns.structural_signature: A persistent specification slot, separate from turn-level content, is applied to every generated turn. Changing only that slot changes the voice and role of all subsequent output while task, inputs, and every other interface element stay fixed; the slot is a controlled variable of the system, not a property of any one response.
patterns.source_pattern_name: persona or stance assigned to the agent
patterns.description: persona or stance assigned to the agent

patterns.short_summary: A procedure defined over two or more roles is run by one person alone, with the model filling every role but theirs.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Converts a coordinated group activity into a single-user experience supported by AI roles.
patterns.definition: A procedure defined over two or more roles is run by one person alone, with the model filling every role but theirs. The scheduling and co-presence requirements disappear; the activity becomes asynchronous and single-user. The interaction retains the shape of the multi-party original.
patterns.structural_signature: The system takes a procedure defined over n≥2 human participants and reassigns all roles but one to the model, leaving a single-user loop that runs at the remaining participant's own pace. Structurally: role count unchanged, human count reduced to one, synchronization constraint removed. Observable in the paper as a mapping from the multi-party procedure's roles onto the agent's behaviours. Transplants to pair programming, moderated review, negotiation practice, peer critique.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the model fills all but one role of a multi-party procedure
patterns.description: the model fills all but one role of a multi-party procedure

patterns.short_summary: The system generates a bounded scenario and places the user inside it as a participant rather than as an operator addressing a tool.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Frames interaction as role-play inside a bounded situation rather than tool operation.
patterns.definition: The system generates a bounded scenario and places the user inside it as a participant rather than as an operator addressing a tool. The user acts in role, and the model plays the other parties or the environment; the run can be repeated. What the user produces during the run is behaviour in the scenario, not a request to the model.
patterns.structural_signature: Control flow: a setup step fixes the scenario's parameters (topic, role, self-representation), after which the interface switches into an in-scenario mode where the user's turns are read as actions of a participant and the model's turns are read as the world's response. The scenario has an entry and an exit, and re-entry restarts it rather than continuing it. The signature is the *frame switch* — user input stops being instructions to a system and becomes conduct inside a generated world. Transplants to sales rehearsal, incident drills, or a generated market a strategy is tested against.
patterns.source_pattern_name: a generated scenario the user enters as a participant
patterns.description: a generated scenario the user enters as a participant

patterns.short_summary: More than one party is present at the same system instance at the same time — two humans, a dyad, a group, or humans plus a population of agents — and the design allocates distinct roles among them.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Organizes a shared experience for multiple humans, agents, or mixed groups.
patterns.definition: More than one party is present at the same system instance at the same time — two humans, a dyad, a group, or humans plus a population of agents — and the design allocates distinct roles among them. The system is addressed to the configuration rather than to a single user.
patterns.structural_signature: At least two simultaneous role slots on one system instance, each with its own input rights, and system behavior that depends on which role acted. Removing one participant leaves the interaction structurally incomplete — a role goes unfilled — rather than merely reducing the number of users.
patterns.source_pattern_name: several co-present participants around one system
patterns.description: several co-present participants around one system Two humans, a dyad, a group, or one person plus a simulated population.

patterns.short_summary: The object the user is authoring is instantiated as a conversational agent, and the user develops it by talking to it in character rather than by editing a representation of it.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Collapses editing and testing into conversation with the artifact itself.
patterns.definition: The object the user is authoring is instantiated as a conversational agent, and the user develops it by talking to it in character rather than by editing a representation of it. Answers the agent gives become part of the object's specification. Editing and testing collapse into the same act.
patterns.structural_signature: The work object's current specification is bound to an agent's conditioning; the user's only interaction surface with that object is dialogue with the agent so conditioned; the agent's replies are treated as further content of the object, feeding back into the specification. Structurally: the artifact's state and the interlocutor's state are the same state, and there is no separate editable rendering of the object. Transplants wherever an artifact can be voiced — a product spec interviewed as a "customer", a policy queried as itself.
patterns.source_pattern_name: the artifact under construction embodied as the interlocutor
patterns.description: the artifact under construction embodied as the interlocutor

patterns.short_summary: One system presents deliberately different surfaces to different classes of participant, so what each party can see and do depends on their role.
patterns.ui_ux_rationale: Gives participant classes different views, information, controls, or communication channels over shared state.
patterns.definition: One system presents deliberately different surfaces to different classes of participant, so what each party can see and do depends on their role. The asymmetry is designed rather than incidental: some information is withheld from one side, or an extra channel exists for the other. The parties nonetheless act on a shared underlying state.
patterns.structural_signature: A single backend serves two or more role-specific front-ends or channels whose contents differ by construction; a role assignment determines which view a session receives; at least one channel is private to one role. State written by any role is visible to the others only through their own role's view.
patterns.source_pattern_name: role-asymmetric surfaces over one system
patterns.description: role-asymmetric surfaces over one system

factors.definition: The person holds a goal that is clear to them but cannot state it precisely or completely enough for the system to act on it. This is the gulf of envisioning: specification is incremental and partly unknowable in advance, so the person must externalise a fuzzy intention before any output is possible.
factors.boundary_rule: Ends at the moment an output exists: F1 is about getting the system to a first attempt at all, F2 about moving between or beyond attempts. Nearest sibling: F2 (Creativity Support and Ideation).

sub_factors.definition: The difficulty a person has in putting something they hold internally — an intent, a felt reaction, a quality criterion, a piece of advice — into an explicit form another party can act on. The person is taken to know, at some level, what they want; the claimed problem is the conversion into words, parameters, or a stated principle. It is a difficulty of expression, not of deciding.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. The corpus names it as a difficulty, a burden of conversion, or a "not straightforward" task. A minority of assertions state the complementary capacity in recognition terms (helping a person notice rather than generate), but the framing is still built on the stated difficulty.

sub_factors.definition: The person does not hold a fully formed goal at the moment they must specify one; what they want is partly constructed, and revised, through the act of working on the task. Papers claim their designs engage the condition in which a target is under-specified at the outset and shifts as the person sees intermediate results. The factor concerns the state of the goal itself, not the difficulty of putting an already-held goal into words.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus frames vagueness as a defect of the specification moment ("despite inherently vague, fluid, and evolving intents") and equally as a legitimate developmental process worth protecting (preference construction, problem-solution co-evolution).

sub_factors.definition: Getting from a stated goal to the ordered set of sub-goals or steps that would achieve it, and holding that structure while acting on it. The claimed difficulty is that people cannot break their own objective into separable parts, or cannot sustain long-range planning across the many steps a complex outcome requires. It transplants to any goal too large to be accomplished in one move.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: implicit expression of attention and intent
sub_factors.definition: While a person works, their behaviour continuously leaks where they are looking and what they are after, without their having stated any of it. The factor is this unspoken behavioural signal — gaze, dwell, pointer movement, or comparable traces — treated as a readable expression of attention and intent rather than as mere input. It concerns what the person conveys without deliberate articulation.

Before anything can be solved, the person has to settle what the problem is — which constraints count, what would qualify as an answer, and where the boundaries of the task lie. The factor is that constitutive act of framing, held apart from and prior to solving. It concerns the formulation of the problem, in any domain where the problem is not given ready-made.

factors.definition: The person cannot tell what range of outputs is achievable and cannot move a produced artifact closer to intent without losing coherence or control. Both halves are the same creativity-support work of ideation within an output space the person can only see by generating in it.
factors.boundary_rule: Presupposes at least one output exists; F1 covers the case where the person cannot yet get the system to produce anything on target. Nearest sibling: F1 (Gulf of Envisioning).

sub_factors.definition: The person's capacity to generate, vary, and explore possibilities of their own, and the value the corpus places on that exploratory activity as an activity. Papers claim designs support idea generation, early-stage exploration, iteration on one's own concepts, and the searching through which discovery is said to happen. The unit is the person's generative activity, not the novelty of any artifact produced.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY. Stated as something to support, enable, or preserve — creative writing, rapid ideation, early-stage exploration, "a playground for users to explore".

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: need for external inspiration and examples
sub_factors.definition: The claim that people cannot reliably produce ideas from nothing and must go outside themselves — to references, precedents, or examples — to get moving or to get past a stall. Papers state it as blockage, as the cost of starting from scratch, or as an established practice of consulting outside material. The factor is the dependence on external stimulus, not the quality of ideas eventually produced.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. The corpus states it as a difficulty (writer's block, the challenge of "conceiving vivid graphical design" from scratch, exploration being costly) and as a positively named human need ("inspiration" as the dimension the system is framed around).

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: iterative rather than linear creative process
sub_factors.definition: Creative work does not run start-to-finish; the person cycles between making, looking around, and reworking, and may re-enter an earlier stage at any point. The factor is this non-linear temporal shape of the person's process, asserted as the proper form of the work rather than as an inefficiency. It concerns how the activity is sequenced, not how much of it there is.

Beyond the particular option in front of them, a person needs a sense of the field of possible options — what else could exist, and how the alternatives are laid out relative to each other. The factor is the person's grasp of that space of possibilities for the problem they face. It concerns a map of what is possible, not the production of any one candidate.

The cost of reaching an acceptable result by repeated attempts because the relation between what the person supplies and what comes back cannot be predicted. Papers frame it as random, laborious, or requiring many candidates before one is usable, and as demanding persistence from the person. It is the iteration itself that is claimed to be burdensome, not the difficulty of any single attempt.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Named as a laborious, random, or inefficient process, and as requiring persistence — with a secondary framing of serendipity as the reason many attempts are needed.

sub_factors.definition: The person must satisfy several requirements at once that pull against each other, and every choice of what to include or leave out trades one off against another. The claimed difficulty is the simultaneity: no single requirement is hard, but they cannot all be maximized. It transplants to any selection or composition task governed by more than one binding constraint.

The narrowing of what a person considers or produces as a consequence of what they were shown. Papers frame it as fixation — being captured by an example so the space of options shrinks — and as convergence across people who all draw on the same source, reducing the variety of what a group collectively produces. The claim is about the person's range narrowing, not about any single output being poor.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Stated as an undesirable outcome — fixation, focus drift, hindered creativity, diminished diversity of results.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: tension between precise control and surprise
sub_factors.definition: A person sometimes wants exactly what they specified and sometimes wants to be shown something they would not have specified, and the same encounter cannot fully serve both. The factor is this conflict inside the person's own wants — fidelity to a stated criterion against variety and unexpectedness — which the interface must resolve without knowing which mode the person is in. It is a conflict of goals, not a shortage of control.

Recognizing that a structure in one domain matches a structure in an unrelated one, and carrying it across. Papers frame this as a cognitive capacity people cannot exercise on demand: finding a fitting source is hard, and understanding a retrieved one well enough to build from it is a further difficulty. It transplants to any task solved by importing a structure from elsewhere.

factors.definition: The person has produced something they judge imperfect but cannot tell what specifically to change. They need actionable feedback addressed to the artifact, at a grain fine enough to act on.
factors.boundary_rule: Presupposes the person already knows there is a problem; F8 covers not noticing one. Nearest sibling: F8 (Metacognition).

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: need for direction while stuck, and uptake of direction offered
sub_factors.definition: The person needs direction on how to proceed at the moment they are stuck, and whether they take up direction that is offered is itself variable. Papers claim their designs engage the absence of timely in-task support and the person's receptivity to it. The concern is being shown a way forward while working, not acquiring durable competence.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus states absence of support as a deficit (lack of visual guidance, lack of timely help when confusion arises) and receptivity or uptake of guidance as a human disposition in its own right.

sub_factors.definition: The person cannot get sufficient purchase on their own work from the inside, and the outside judgment they need is scarce, slow, or unavailable at the moment of work. The factor is the standing demand for a critical second view on an artifact the person themselves produced, and the cost structure that keeps such a view from arriving when it would matter. Claimed by the authors as the human condition their design engages; not independently verified here.

factors.definition: The person faces more content than they can read, remember, or traverse, and cannot locate, condense, or connect it into something they can act on. The difficulty is sensemaking over volume itself, independent of whether the material is trustworthy.
factors.boundary_rule: Is about comprehending a mass of material; F3 is about validating a claim drawn from it. Nearest sibling: F3 (Judgment and Decision Making).

sub_factors.definition: The person's grasp of content that is dense, technical, or outside their expertise — what it says, what it implies, and what matters in it. Papers frame the difficulty as arising from the material and the reader's distance from it, and frame comprehension as the human dimension the design engages. The object understood is subject matter, not machinery.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. Comprehension is named as the capacity to support ("improve comprehension", "support code understanding") and its absence as the stated problem ("most people do not have the domain expertise", descriptions that "do not adequately describe important insights").

sub_factors.definition: The cost of finding the relevant material inside a large, fragmented, or linear body of sources before any work on it can begin. Papers frame this as manual scanning, sifting, or locating, and sometimes as the inverse capacity of encountering material one would not have thought to look for. It transplants to any corpus a person must get through to reach the few items that matter.

The person imposes structure on open-ended material whose organising shape is not given in advance, moving in branching, parallel cycles between gathering and interpreting. Papers claim their designs engage this structuring work, including the difficulty of pulling scattered material into a coherent account. What is at stake is the construction of an organisation, not the absorption of one already present in the material.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY — the corpus describes sensemaking, foraging, and narrative construction as the analytic and interpretive work people do, with its branching structure framed as resistant to automation rather than as a defect.

sub_factors.definition: Retrieval of specific past content — what was said, decided, done, or lived through — at the moment the person needs it. Papers claim their designs engage the difficulty of getting particular prior material back into mind, and in some cases the emotional cost of doing so. The object is content that existed earlier and must be brought back, not structure the person must currently hold.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus states recall as a target to be raised (information recall, being reminded of overlooked material) and as a difficulty in its own right (rationale that cannot be recalled in real time, memories that are demanding to retrieve).

sub_factors.definition: The person's arrival at new understanding or new connections that were not stated anywhere in the material they were given. The claimed difficulty is that the person receives conclusions rather than being able to explore and draw their own, or that forming and validating candidate understandings across scattered material is costly. It transplants to any body of material a person is expected to learn something new from.

Within material the person already has in front of them, telling which elements carry the significance and which are incidental. The claimed difficulty is that significance is not marked in the artifact, so consequential detail goes unnoticed, particularly for those without the experience to know where to look. It transplants to any artifact whose important parts are not visually or structurally distinguished from its unimportant ones.

As a body of work grows, the person loses hold of its overall shape and drifts into local detail, unable to see how the parts relate or where they are within the whole. Papers claim their designs engage this loss of overview and orientation. The material is present and available; what fails is the person's grasp of its structure.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM — the corpus states this as difficulty and drift: hard to oversee a growing draft, hard to track how parts connect, tempting to revise locally, pushed toward implementation detail instead of the shape of the design.

sub_factors.definition: People make sense of what they are doing now by reaching backward into what has happened and forward into what might, and this looking across time is treated as work in its own right. The factor is the person's prospective and retrospective cognition — the construction of meaning and agency out of past and future — rather than the storage or retrieval of facts about either.

Working something out and telling someone about it make incompatible demands on the same material: the trace that supports discovery is messy in exactly the ways an audience-facing account must not be. The factor is the person's position between these two modes and the cost of converting the artifact of one into the artifact of the other. Papers frame it as a tension or gap rather than as a sequence of steps.

factors.definition: The person must decide whether to act on what the system returned — whether it is correct, whether it bears on what they asked for, and by what standard it should be judged at all. The difficulty is the labour and the basis of that judgment: checking can cost as much as doing the work unaided, the criteria are often unsettled, and the decision has to be made at a particular moment whether or not the grounds are in hand.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns the person's judgment of a returned output and the decision that follows from it. F4 concerns visibility into the process that produced it, whether or not any output is in question. Nearest sibling: F4 (Oversight).

sub_factors.definition: The work left to a person of checking whether something produced for them is correct, adequate, or acceptable before they can use it. Papers frame this as labour that has been displaced rather than removed: producing is cheaper, so checking becomes the bottleneck. The factor is the human checking work, not any property of what generated the output.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Named as a burden that "remains on the end-user", as effort "shifted" rather than removed, and as an inability to check when only a final result is shown.

sub_factors.definition: A person must commit to a choice at a particular moment, and whether they hold the information that bears on it at that moment is what is at stake. The factor is the person's capacity to decide on an adequate basis at the point of decision, where the relevant material is otherwise dispersed, absent, or arriving too late to act on. It concerns the act of choosing, not the act of understanding for its own sake.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: judging whether returned material bears on the need
sub_factors.definition: What the system returns may not be about what the person actually wanted, and the person is left to judge the fit between the two. Papers claim their designs engage the gap between a request and the returned material, and the judgment of relevance the person must exercise over candidates. This is a property of the match, not of the correctness of the content.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus frames off-target output as a harm (focus drift, unresolved intent-outcome gaps) and also frames relevance judgment as an activity the person performs over candidates.

sub_factors.definition: The condition in which a person must judge something without a settled or stably applied standard: what counts as good is contested, depends on who is judging, or drifts within one judge over a long session. Papers frame the consequence as judgments that cannot be replicated or defended. It concerns the standard being unclear, not the effort of applying a clear one.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Framed as subjectivity, unfairness, narrowness of available measures, and lack of replicability — conditions to be remedied.

sub_factors.definition: People can be moved to false beliefs or unwanted decisions by content that is wrong, fallacious, or engineered to persuade, and they vary in how far they resist it. Papers claim their designs engage this vulnerability and the counterpart capacity to withstand it. The factor is the person's exposure and resistance to persuasive falsehood, whatever the source of that content.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus names susceptibility, echo chambers, and damaged public trust as harms, and resistance to misinformation and critical examination of content as capacities to be strengthened.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: linking information back to its referent
sub_factors.definition: A statement can be perfectly clear on its own terms and still be unusable because the person cannot tell which part of the object it is about. The factor is the interpretive gap the person must close between a piece of information and the thing that information concerns, when the two are presented apart from each other. Papers frame this as a gulf of evaluation to be narrowed rather than as a property of the information itself.

The posture a person takes toward what the system produced — whether they treat it as a candidate to be judged right or wrong, as raw material to build on, or as a constraint or resource to work within. The claimed difficulty is that the output's surface properties push the person into a stance that does not serve the task. It transplants to any setting where a person must decide what kind of thing an automatically produced artifact is to them.

The person receives an answer whose underlying confidence is not visible in the answer's surface form, and must decide how much weight to place on it. The factor is the human's handling of stated or unstated uncertainty — whether a spread of possibilities rather than a single value reaches them, and how their own numerical and probabilistic fluency conditions what they do with it. It is about the recipient's position under uncertainty, not about the mechanism that produces the uncertainty.

factors.definition: The person cannot see what the system did, is doing, or is about to do, and so cannot form a working model of it, anticipate it, or supervise it. The difficulty is the legibility of the process and of the system's competence — including, at the limit, whether the person can tell a system was involved at all.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns the person's view into the process and the model of the system they build from it. F3 concerns adjudicating a finished output. Nearest sibling: F3 (Judgment and Decision Making).

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: the person's understanding of how an output was produced
sub_factors.definition: The person's ability to see how a result was arrived at — what was considered, what was discarded, and why this outcome rather than another. Papers frame the absence as under-explanation and the presence as understanding, transparency, or the person being able to relate their own inputs to the outcome. It concerns the derivation of a result, not the subject matter the result is about.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. The corpus states it as a capacity to be enabled ("understanding and assessment of the recommended items") and as a deficit ("under-explored and under-explained").

sub_factors.definition: What the person believes an automated counterpart is able and unable to do, and how that belief forms and shifts across repeated use. Papers frame the deficit as opacity — the person cannot tell what is achievable, so failures arrive unexpectedly — and the capacity as adaptation, where experience accumulates into workable expectations. It is a belief the person holds, not a documented property of the system.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. The corpus frames it as a deficit (capability "is opaque to the user", the "Gulf of Envisioning", unexpected failures) and as a capacity (users adapt and build up experience across interactions).

sub_factors.definition: Before or during joint work, the person must form expectations about what an autonomous counterpart will do next, or how it will behave across situations they have not yet encountered, in order to plan their own actions. Papers claim their designs engage this forward-looking prediction problem and the difficulty of getting evidence for it in advance. The concern is future behaviour, not explanation of behaviour already observed.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM — the corpus states this as an inability: feedback on behaviour is unavailable before deployment, behaviour across the input range is hard to understand, and problems surface only when they are expensive.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: awareness of AI involvement and provenance
sub_factors.definition: Whether the person can tell that a machine was involved at all, what it did, and which parts of what they are looking at came from it. The claimed difficulty is that machine involvement is not perceptible in the artifact or the interaction, so the person cannot attribute origin without being told. It applies wherever an output's authorship or generation history bears on how a person should treat it.

factors.definition: The person cannot see flaws, biases, or blind spots in their own reasoning or work without an external mirror, and does not notice when they should stop and check. The gap is metacognitive — in self-monitoring — so it cannot be closed by giving the person more information.
factors.boundary_rule: Is about not knowing that something is wrong; F9 is about knowing it is and not knowing what to change. Nearest sibling: F9 (Guidance and Feedback).

sub_factors.definition: The person's capacity to turn attention back on themselves — their own process, decisions, feelings, or conduct — and to notice something about it they had not articulated. Papers claim designs engage this by provoking moments of reflection, replaying what the person did, or prompting inquiry rather than supplying answers. The object of attention is the person, not the material or the system.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY. Consistently framed as reflection to be supported, provoked, or made possible; the corpus does not frame it as a deficit.

sub_factors.definition: The person's capacity to question, examine, and weigh what is put in front of them rather than take it at face value. Papers claim designs invoke this by presenting alternative perspectives, by prompting reconsideration during reading, or by making a claim available for scrutiny. It is directed outward at content, claims, or the arrangement being examined.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY. Framed as a skill to invoke, build, or provoke — critical thinking, critical re-examination, reflective engagement.

sub_factors.definition: Whether a person encounters viewpoints other than the ones already available to them, and whether those viewpoints are preserved rather than collapsed. Papers frame the deficit as narrowing — echo chambers, polarization, lack of access to varied others — and the capacity as perspective expansion or considering alternate readings. It transplants to any setting where the range of positions a person meets shapes what they conclude.

The person's ability to judge accurately what they do and do not know, and to plan, monitor, and adjust their own effort on that basis. Papers claim their designs engage this second-order control over one's own learning, including the miscalibration — typically overconfidence — that undermines it. The object of judgment is the person's own state of knowing, not the material or the system.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus names metacognition, self-regulation, and calibration as skills to be strengthened, and overconfidence and inability to plan one's own study as the deficits designs target.

factors.definition: The person cannot gauge how much of their judgment to hand over, and hands over more than they intended, so their own scrutiny and effort erode. Overreliance is a standing disposition toward the system rather than a judgment about any one output.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns global reliance and effort; F3 concerns the act of checking one specific output. Nearest sibling: F3 (Judgment and Decision Making).

sub_factors.definition: The person's willingness to credit an automated counterpart and the attitudes that support or undermine it. Papers name trust as a stated aim or evaluation dimension, and name mistrust — driven by privacy worries, incorrect output, or bias — as the condition to be addressed. The factor is the person's attitude, not the counterpart's reliability.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. The corpus states trust as something to gain, improve, or measure, and also states mistrust as a persisting problem the design confronts.

sub_factors.definition: Whether a person's reliance on an automated counterpart matches how far it should be relied on in the case at hand. Papers frame the harm as accepting output without scrutiny, so the person's performance is capped by the system's, and frame the target capacity as appropriate or calibrated reliance. The subject is the person's disposition to accept, not the accuracy of what is being accepted.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. The harm framing dominates (overreliance, unwarranted confidence, confirmation bias); the same papers state the paired capacity as "appropriate reliance" or appropriately calibrated trust.

sub_factors.definition: People systematically take the lower-effort option even when a more effortful one would serve them better, and papers treat this preference as a fixed condition any design must survive rather than something to argue against. The claimed harm is that convenience drives shallow engagement, over-disclosure, or effort minimization. It transplants to any setting where the easy path and the good path diverge.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: accountability and ethics of delegating judgment
sub_factors.definition: When a judgment that carries consequences for someone is handed to a machine, it becomes unclear who answers for the result, and whether handing it over was permissible at all. Papers frame this as clarifying responsibility across asymmetric parties, or as the ethical concerns practitioners raise about delegating an assessment. It transplants to any consequential decision a person could either make or pass on.

factors.definition: The person cannot tell whether an output or representation skews against groups of people, nor steer it toward what they judge fair. The difficulty is the inability to audit and adjust for bias, not the presence of skew in the model.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns systematic skew across groups; F12 concerns one identified individual's likely reaction. Nearest sibling: F12 (Perspective-Taking).

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: awareness of bias, one's own and encoded
sub_factors.definition: Skew that is present but unnoticed — in the person's own assumptions, in the norms carried by the material they work with, or in the outputs they accept — and the difficulty of bringing it into view. Papers claim their designs engage noticing, prioritising, and reasoning about such skew. The factor is the person's awareness, not the existence of the skew.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus states blind spots and overlooked biases as deficits, and recognition of bias, awareness of encoded norms, and fair representation as capacities the design engages.

factors.definition: Acting on generated output can hurt someone, and the person may not see the harm coming or may carry the burden of answering for it afterwards. The factor covers exposure to harm, harm noticed too late, physical safety and error, and the work of demonstrating compliance.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns consequences the person bears or must answer for. F5 concerns the disposition to defer to the system that can produce them. Nearest sibling: F5 (Appropriate Reliance).

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: exposure to harm from acting on generated output
sub_factors.definition: The person stands to be hurt, or to hurt something they care about, if they act on what the system produced. Papers frame the human dimension as the exposure the person carries and must guard against — physical breakage, psychological injury, an unacceptable output reaching a vulnerable recipient. It transplants to any setting where acting on an automated suggestion has consequences the person cannot undo.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: unawareness of a harm until too late
sub_factors.definition: A consequence of the person's own activity is invisible or unfamiliar at the moment of acting, so it cannot enter their decision until after the fact. Papers frame the target as raising awareness of a harm, cost, or risk the population is said not to know about. It transplants to any setting where the effect of an action is displaced in time, scale, or visibility from the action itself.

People make mistakes and lapse in attention while acting, and in some settings a mistake injures someone or breaks something. The factor is the person's own error-proneness and the bodily or operational consequence attached to it. It transplants to any activity where a slip by the person has a cost beyond needing to redo the step.

Beyond doing the work, a person must produce an artifact whose function is to prove to a supervising party that the work was done to requirement. The factor is that second, documentary obligation and the labour it adds — an artifact shaped by an auditor's demands rather than by the task's own needs. It concerns answering to an authority, not the difficulty of the underlying task.

factors.definition: What the task costs the person to carry out: time and repeated manual effort, the mental load of holding it together, the friction of an interface that has to be figured out, and the attention it demands or erodes. The factor is the expenditure itself, whatever the task is for.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns the cost of doing the work. F20 concerns whether the person has the capability to do it at all. Nearest sibling: F20 (Skill and Self-Efficacy).

sub_factors.definition: The labour a task costs a person, counted in time, repetition, tedium, or fatigue. The claim is that a person must expend more of themselves on the task than the task is worth, or that the expenditure is misallocated toward overhead. It is about the quantity of work demanded, not about how hard that work is to think through.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Consistently a burden to be reduced, shifted, or reallocated — "time-consuming and tedious", "burdensome", "survey fatigue", "administrative overhead".

sub_factors.definition: The mental processing a task demands of a person at once — holding material in mind, integrating scattered pieces, or working through more information than can be handled. Papers claim this demand degrades the quality of what people do or crowds out the judgment they should be spending attention on. It is about processing demand, not about elapsed time or missing training.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Uniformly stated as load to be lowered, overload to be relieved, or burden that degrades response quality.

sub_factors.definition: How fast and how well the work gets done — throughput, speed of producing an artifact, and measured quality of performance on the task. The factor covers both units to which that outcome is attributed: the individual person's own speed and quality at their own task, and the joint result produced by a person and a system working together where the paper treats the outcome as a property of the pairing rather than of either party alone. Both readings are coded here, and which one is at issue is read off the paper's own attribution; the joint reading additionally requires a claim about the pairing, such as that neither the person's skill nor the system's standalone accuracy predicts the joint outcome. Papers claim their designs engage this as the headline human dimension, stated in terms of the process being sped up or the performance being better. The factor is the observable performance of the work, not the person's felt exertion in doing it.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY — the corpus states this as a gain to be had (efficiency, speed, versatility, human performance), with slowness framed as the limitation of existing tooling.

sub_factors.definition: What it costs the person to work the thing: how much effort goes into figuring out what to do, how fluently the action they intend becomes the action the system takes, and how satisfied they are with the doing of it. The factor is the person's experience of operating an instrument — the same difficulty anyone has driving an unfamiliar machine — and it transplants to any operable artifact, with or without a model behind it. It is coded only from claims about what the person experienced or reported; a designer's assertion that the interface is simple is not evidence for it, and neither is any property attributed to the artifact rather than to the person using it.

A finite attentional resource has to be directed at what matters and sustained there, across competing demands and against declining alertness. Papers claim their designs engage the allocation of attention, the drift away from the target, and the alertness the person can hold over time. The concern is the person's ongoing attentional state, whatever is competing for it.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus states distraction, divided attention, and fatigue-impaired alertness as deficits, and attentiveness to content and low attentional demand as properties to be raised or protected.

factors.definition: The task demands expertise the person does not have, or the encounter is meant to build it. The factor covers the barrier itself, the learning and skill acquisition that closes it, and the person's own belief that they are capable of the task.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns capability and its growth. F19 concerns what the work costs someone who already has the capability. Nearest sibling: F19 (Effort and Cognitive Load).

sub_factors.definition: The claim that a task demands training, proficiency, or specialist judgment that the intended person does not have, so the task is closed to them or done worse. It covers steep learning curves, tools built for specialists, and stated gaps between novices and experts. The person's competence, not the interface's clarity, is what the paper says is missing.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM. Stated as a lack, a steep curve, an exclusion, or a gap between novice and expert performance.

sub_factors.definition: The person's acquisition of knowledge, skill, or practice that they carry away from the interaction. Papers claim designs engage this by giving examples, feedback, simulated practice, or exposure to how others do the task, and some claim it as something a design must be careful not to supplant. What distinguishes it is that the person is meant to end up more capable, not merely to have finished the task.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY. Stated as learning gains, learning outcomes, learning strategies, or learning to be protected from short-circuiting.

sub_factors.definition: The person's belief in their own ability to do the thing, and their confidence in the judgments they reach. Papers frame the deficit as a felt sense of failure or low perceived competence that keeps people from attempting or persisting, and the capacity as confidence to approach a task or to commit to a decision. It is a belief about oneself, not about a system.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. Deficit framings (sense of failure, low self-efficacy, low perceived competence as a demotivating factor) sit alongside capacity framings (confidence to approach, updating one's own judgment with higher confidence).

factors.definition: The person is working alongside something that does part of the work, and what is at stake is how much of the direction stays theirs. It covers holding the wheel over an automated process, the share of the task left to them once the work is split, what their role becomes as a result, and the interruptions, waits and broken threads that come with an activity they no longer fully pace.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns who directs the work and what the person is left holding. F4 concerns whether they can see what the system did with the latitude it has. Nearest sibling: F4 (Oversight).

sub_factors.definition: The person's claimed capacity to direct what an automated process does and to remain the one deciding, rather than receiving a result they did not shape. Papers state it as control, steering, autonomy, empowerment, or ownership of the decision, and state its absence as limited control or as automation encroaching on the person's role. It is about who holds the wheel, independent of what the output is.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH. The dominant framing is a CAPACITY to be served (control, ownership, efficacy, steering as something users want); the corpus also frames its loss as a harm — "limited user control", and "the tension between automation and scholarly agency".

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: collaborative roles and the work left to the person
sub_factors.definition: A piece of work that the person could have done alone is split between them and a system, and the split settles what the person is left holding — which parts of the task stay theirs, and whether what stays is the part worth doing or the residue. The factor is the person's difficulty and capacity under that allocation: getting a share of the work that is meaningful to them, taking up whatever the system hands back, and covering whatever the split leaves uncovered. It transplants to any setting where part of a person's work is taken over by something else — a delegate, an assistant, an earlier generation of automation — and it is coded from claims about the person's portion, never from a description of how the system's own roles were configured.

An externally timed intrusion pulls a person out of ongoing work, or the work itself is fragmented across threads and contexts so that continuity is repeatedly broken. Papers claim their designs engage the cost of being taken out of flow and the risk that any offered help is intrusive. The trigger lies outside the person's own attentional effort, which is what makes this distinct from failing to stay focused.
sub_factors.framing: DEFICIT/HARM — every central assertion in the packet states this as a cost: disruption, intrusion, fragmentation, being pulled out of the workflow, or being sidelined.

sub_factors.definition: The claim that some part of a task rests on knowledge, context, or judgment that only the particular human holds, so automation can supplement but not stand in for them. Papers state it as tasks requiring human insight, as contextual knowledge an outsider or a machine lacks, and as augmentation rather than replacement. It is a claim about what the person uniquely contributes, not about a system's accuracy.
sub_factors.framing: CAPACITY. The human contribution is the thing being asserted and protected — domain knowledge, educational insight, expert interpretation, capability enhancement rather than replacement.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: shift in the human's role and practice
sub_factors.definition: When part of a person's work is taken over, what remains of their role is not simply less of the same but a different job, with different competences at its centre. The factor is this reallocation of what the person is there to do — the move from one mode of practice to another — as the dimension the paper says its design engages. It concerns the shape of the person's role, not their skill level within it.

An exchange that runs long enough, or resumes often enough, stops holding together: what was established earlier no longer bears on what happens now, and the person must re-establish ground they had already laid. The factor is the human's experience of coherence and completeness across an extended or multi-session engagement, and the burden of repair when that coherence lapses. It concerns the thread of the interaction, not the person's own memory.

Work that involves a slow-producing partner puts the person into stretches of dead time they must inhabit, not merely tolerate. The factor is the human experience of waiting — what the person does, feels, and attends to during a pause they did not choose and cannot shorten. It is the temporal experience on the person's side, not the duration figure itself.

Some reasoning tasks depend on what the person has not yet been told: the order of disclosure, and the withholding of certain facts until earned, is a precondition for the inference the person is trying to make. The factor is the person's dependence on paced, structured release of information, and the collapse of their reasoning when material arrives out of order or too early. It concerns the sequencing of what reaches the person, not the truth of it.

factors.definition: The person cannot predict how another specific person will perceive, react to, or need something, so misjudges what to make for them. The difficulty is a limit on perspective-taking toward a particular other.
factors.boundary_rule: Concerns one identified other person; F18 concerns systematic skew across groups of people. Nearest sibling: F18 (Bias and Fairness).

sub_factors.definition: A person and a counterpart they are working with — another person or a system — hold different conceptions of the same thing, and the gap between those conceptions has to be closed for the work to proceed. The factor is the person's side of establishing that common ground: converging on a shared reference, adapting to the counterpart as it adapts to them, and fitting the counterpart's contributions into their own cognitive and creative process. The parties are mutually reachable and can negotiate meaning with each other, which is what distinguishes this from addressing a public; whether the counterpart is a person or a system does not bear on the coding, and difficulty of integrating a machine counterpart's contributions is evidence here on the same footing as miscommunication between two people.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus names representational gaps, miscommunication, and expressive suppression as harms, and grounded communication, partnership, co-creativity, bidirectional alignment, and shared mental states as capacities the work depends on; integration difficulty is framed as what stands in the way of that capacity.

sub_factors.definition: Whether what a person produces lands with people who are not present during its production — whether it reaches them at all, holds them, and is taken the way it was meant. Papers claim their designs engage the producer's problem of anticipating and affecting an absent receiving public. The receivers are a body the producer cannot interrogate, which is what separates this from any face-to-face understanding problem.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus frames reach and audience engagement as things to be raised, and audience misinterpretation and its societal consequences as a harm the producer must anticipate.

sub_factors.definition: One person's grasp of another person's inner state — their goals, feelings, or reading of a situation — when that state is not directly observable and must be inferred. Papers claim their designs engage both the inference itself and the affective response that follows it. The other party is a human whose perspective is the object of understanding, not a co-worker whose actions need coordinating.
sub_factors.framing: BOTH — the corpus names empathy and mutual understanding as capacities to be raised, and simultaneously names imagination gaps and misinterpretation of the other party as failures the design targets.

sub_factors.definition: Whether what a person says fits the relationship, the culture, and the moment, over and above being clear or well formed. The claimed demand is that fluency is not sufficient: an utterance must be calibrated to who is receiving it and what stands between them. It transplants to any communication addressed to a particular person in a particular relation.

factors.definition: In a live shared activity participation goes lopsided, disagreement stays unresolved, and no one manages turns or surfaces quiet contributions. The difficulty is the missing structure of the exchange, not the absence of participants.
factors.boundary_rule: Is about who speaks during the activity; F17 is about who owns and sees what afterward. Nearest sibling: F17 (Privacy and Ownership).

sub_factors.definition: When several people work on the same thing at the same time, they must divide labour, take turns, and adjust to each other's moves, and the quality of that meshing is itself at stake. The factor is the observable conduct of joint work between people — who does what, in what order, and how the group's strategy settles. It concerns behaviour among humans, whatever the task.

sub_factors.sub_factor_name: minority voice and psychological safety in groups
sub_factors.definition: In a group where influence is unevenly distributed, holding a dissenting view and being able to say it are different things, and the second carries a social cost the first does not. The factor is whether a person in the weaker position feels safe enough to voice a divergent opinion, and the conformity and groupthink that follow when they do not. "Minority" here is a position in the group's power structure, not a demographic category.
